newsitem.title: USA: New Prozac use seen as a boost for Lilly.
newsitem.headline: New Prozac use seen as a boost for Lilly.

text.p: Eli Lilly & Co, which received approval Monday to market its antidepressant drug Prozac to treat bulimia nervosa, an eating disorder, may not see a huge gain in sales but will reap benefits nonetheless.
"It will be difficult to assess (the effect on Prozac sales), said Hambrecht & Quist analyst Alex Zisson. "There's not a lot of data on exactly how many people have bulimia."

However, "It's clearly a positive," said Jean Rosenbaum, analyst at PNC Investment Management & Research. "It will help the sales force, give them something new to talk about. It also will keep the drug in the minds of doctors," she said.

Rosenbaum believes the overall impact of the FDA decision will mostly be felt away from Lilly's balance sheet. "It's not a huge leap forward," she said, "but it will have a positive influence on sales."
Lilly received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to market Prozac to treat bulimia nervosa.

Prozac is already the most widely prescribed branded antidepressant in the world, Lilly said. An estimated 24 million people worldwide have used Prozac, including 18 million in the United States, Lilly said.
Prozac was approved for treating clinical depression in the United States in 1987 and to treat obsessive-compulsive behavior in 1994.
Lilly's Prozac is expected to generate 1996 sales of between $2 billion and $2.5 billion, analysts estimate.

"This has been something that Lilly has wanted to do for some time: take their current drugs and expand their uses," said David Lebedeff, an analyst at Raffensperger, Hughes & Co. "Lilly calls it 'leveraging the molecule.'"
"(Marketing Prozac for bulimia treatment) will be a positive," Lebedeff added, "but it's hard to assess the overall impact (on sales)."

An estimated one million Americans, mostly women, suffer from bulimia, Lilly said. The affliction is characterized by recurring episodes of binge-eating followed by self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives or diuretics, or other compusive behavior.
"This comes at a fortuitous time for Lilly," said James Keeney, an analyst at Mabon Securities Corp. "When doctors say 'What's new with Prozac?' they'll have something to talk about."
